Dry run is the default and prints the exact before/after bytes of every edit; --apply repairs one note at a time against the revision its plan was computed from, with per-note outcomes rather than one transaction, and every fix writes an ordinary revision so it is visible in history and revertible. The precondition is not ceremony: the plan's byte offsets describe one specific body, and a span whose bytes are not what the plan recorded is skipped rather than applied at an arbitrary position. non_canonical_link_target runs by default; missing_alt_text is opt-in because a filename is a starting point rather than a description; unlocalized_remote_media is opt-in because it reaches the network and runs the existing localize engine so media policy, SSRF blocking, size/MIME checks and hash rules all apply unchanged. Stale link reference definitions from the plan's list are deliberately not implemented: they are not detected either, since reference definitions are outside the link extractor, so check and fix belong together in a later slice rather than fixing something lint cannot find. A fixture again met the Markdown rule that a space ends an unquoted URL, so [x](Kitchen Plan) truncates - the same rule that decided E1a's slug form, and the fixture now records it.

This is the user's unique-prefix idea applied to the prefix Notrios already has; a new marker like notrios+q: was considered and rejected because it would not help a pasted Obsidian URI (which carries no Notrios prefix) and would add a second link spelling to the 18 non-test files that interpret a target or anchor. Invalid escapes are left exactly as written and + is not a space; %%20 decodes to '% ', matching urllib, which corrected my first test expectation. Block anchors were deliberately left comparing in SQL since block IDs and markers are letters, digits and dashes and never need escaping. The refusals are the feature: merged-cells, ragged-rows, nested-block, multiline-cell, content-outside-table, multiple-tables, no-table, empty-table each return a reason and fall through to the ordinary paste, so nothing a user pastes can be lost - a mangled table is worse than an HTML one because the HTML at least renders, the same rule E3's fix and P7's rewriter follow for a span they cannot place. Wrapper elements (p, div, span, font) are transparent because real pastes are full of them - Google Docs puts a paragraph in every cell - while a second paragraph or a
is multi-line content and is refused rather than flattened into a sentence the author did not write. A link is emitted only when its href survives Markdown: a space ends an unquoted URL and an unescaped ) closes the link early, the same rules E1a and E3 each met in a fixture; otherwise the text is kept and the link dropped, and javascript: is dropped outright. Parsing is DOMParser, which is inert - no scripts run, no resources are fetched - and no HTML is re-emitted; a fixture asserts a script and an onerror in a pasted cell leave no trace and set nothing on window. task: Read-only rather than disabled note title
validation: npm run typecheck && npm test (143) && npm run build
browser verification of the real control plus a disabled-versus-readonly probe
notes: The note title used disabled rather than readOnly when a note could not be edited. Both refuse edits and they are not otherwise interchangeable: A DISABLED INPUT LEAVES THE TAB ORDER, so a Help or trashed note's title could not be focused at all - no caret, no arrow keys, no Home/End, no select-and-copy - and a title longer than the control was unreadable by any means short of resizing the pane. Measured in a browser against a plain non-React probe input to separate the app from the engine: disabled gives focusable:false, readOnly gives focusable:true, and selection and scrolling are identical between them. One difference, and it is the one that matters. Confirmed in the running application: a trashed note's title is readOnly:true, disabled:false, sits at position 12 of 53 in the tab order, and takes focus on click. The CSS selector moved with the attribute (.title-input:disabled to .title-input[readonly]) and gained cursor:text, because the control is read-only rather than inert and styling it as dead would undo in appearance what the attribute fixed in behaviour. The fixture types with @testing-library/user-event rather than fireEvent: fireEvent.change dispatches synthetically and sails straight past readonly, so an assertion built on it would have tested jsdom's laxness rather than the control - it asserts both that no handler fires and that the value is unchanged. Recorded and deliberately not asserted: Chrome does not advance selectionStart on a read-only input though the field still scrolls, reproduced on a plain input outside React, so the obvious test (press End, expect caret at length) would fail for a reason having nothing to do with Notrios; the fixtures assert reachability and selection instead.

notes: POST /api/v1/batch and store.RunBatch apply one bounded organizer transaction - move, add_tags, remove_tags, trash, restore, duplicate - over an explicit note list, in atomic or best_effort mode. Schema v17 adds batch_operations. BOTH OPEN DECISIONS WERE TAKEN RATHER THAN DEFERRED since the task was approved without answers. Idempotency keys are DATABASE-SCOPED AND PERSISTED: an in-memory ledger forgets on restart, which is exactly when a batch is retried, so the key, a sha256 fingerprint of the arguments, and the first run response are stored; a replay returns that response VERBATIM rather than recomputing it against a library that has moved on, and a key reused for different work is refused because answering it would hide a client bug. A DUPLICATE INHERITS CONTENT, NOT IDENTITY: body, notebook, tags and resource references (content-addressed, so sharing a blob is correct), title gains (copy), but never the document_sources row - two notes claiming one imported identity break re-import and trip duplicate_source_id - and never the revision history, since a duplicate should not claim edits that never happened to it. Four item outcomes rather than two: applied, skipped (nothing to do), failed, rolled_back (succeeded then undone by a later failure in an atomic run). Conflating skip with failure makes nothing-to-do look broken and overstates what a run changed; calling a rolled-back item failed blames it for someone else problem. Both modes report EVERY requested item - the modes differ in what a failure does, never in what the report says - and an atomic report is never shorter than its request, with unattempted items carrying a reason. A request that ran is 200 even when every item failed; 4xx is reserved for the call itself being wrong, the same rule E7 applied to malformed query blocks. Preconditions are per item: trash writes a revision so needs a base revision, but per item because a batch is a set of independent notes and one having moved on is not a reason to refuse the rest. A repeated document ID is refused - it would be applied twice, reported twice, and for duplicate would silently make two copies. The lock is held for the whole run, since interleaving another writer between items would make atomic untrue. Nothing reaches a note the single-note surfaces cannot: a test asserts Help notes still refuse to be moved or duplicated by batch. Atomic mode required extracting locked cores from five exported store methods, and the tag helpers gained a did-anything-change return which is what makes an honest skipped possible. TWO DEFECTS CAUGHT BEFORE SHIPPING: ensureSchemaV17 was inserted before ensureSchemaV16 so v16 PRAGMA user_version = 16 ran last and bootstrap reported the wrong version (caught by an existing status test), and duplicate copied document_resource_refs naming a column anchor when it is anchor_json (caught by reading the schema; the compiler cannot see inside a SQL string). The atomic rollback test was verified in both directions - replacing ROLLBACK with COMMIT makes it fail on the assertion that the library is untouched. Out of scope and recorded: stable Markdown-link copy (produces clipboard text rather than changing the library, so not a transaction), a GUI multi-select (F1 is the API; the selection model is UI work F5 will want to share), and MCP exposure (batch tools belong with the organizer profile, F2 - adding them now would put bulk mutation on the default read-only surface). No scale profile: bounded to 500 items, every operation inside is one the single-note surfaces already carry evidence for, and the ledger is a primary-key lookup.

notes: Four cumulative MCP scopes - search-only, read-only (default), editor, organizer - enforced AT THE CALL SITE from the same table that filters tools/list, so the listing and the check cannot disagree. Before F2 only write tools had a call-site guard and every read tool dispatched unconditionally; that was latent rather than live only because no tier existed narrower than read-only. Verified by mutation: deleting the call-site check makes the hidden-tool test fail, and instructively - append_to_note EXECUTES and complains text is required, which is exactly hidden-but-answers-when-called. Four scopes not the roadmap five: administrator is absent by decision since GC, purge, archive restore and publication are unreachable over MCP at any scope, so it would name an empty set; TestNoScopeReachesWholeLibraryOperations asserts that against tool names that do not exist yet, so adding one later fails the test and forces a deliberate choice. Scope not profile because the word already meant two other shipped things - a named local database (notriosctl profile register) and a saved publication selection (notriosctl publish profile save), both of which are a saved named configuration, which is coherent; a permission tier wearing the same word is not, so the permission tier moved. mcp.default_profile is kept as a deprecated alias and when both keys are set THE NARROWER WINS with a log line, because a config key that silently stops applying is bad generally but for this one it would WIDEN what an agent may do, the single direction that must never happen quietly. config.Default() now leaves both keys empty rather than pre-filling the deprecated one, which would have made every default config look half-migrated and emit a deprecation warning nobody caused. An unrecognized value falls back to read-only WITH A WARNING rather than failing closed to the narrowest scope: failing closed is defensible generally, but here a typo would silently disable reading and look like a broken service. An UNCLASSIFIED tool is refused, never defaulted to the narrowest scope - a default would let a tool ship without anyone deciding how much trust it needs, the dangerous kind of safe. TestEveryMCPToolIsClassified fails in both directions: a registered tool with no table entry, and a table entry naming no registered tool. Each scope tool set is asserted as a whole set rather than by spot-checking membership, with editor and organizer asserted as deltas over the tier below plus an explicit cumulativeness check. search-only can see structure (notebook, tag, collection, search-notebook lists) but no note content, because searching by notebook or tag is unusable without them and the line worth drawing is at content. F1 batch surface arrived here as run_batch under organizer, which is where F1 said it belonged. SECURITY_REVIEW records that a scope is a guardrail on ones own agent and not authorization: Notrios is single-user so there is no second principal, the scope lives in the same config file the operator controls, and it is not what makes the endpoint safe to expose - loopback is.

REST gained HTTP Range on resource content. EVERY WITHHELD SURFACE WAS DECIDED RATHER THAN INHERITED - the list was the deliverable - and docs/api/mcp.md now carries a table with a reason per surface (fix, tag rename, notebook deletion, GC, archive operations, publication, purge). The pattern in one sentence: anything that writes outside the note model, deletes permanently, or acts on the whole library at once stays a deliberate act on the command line; batch organizing is the exception that proves it, bounded to an explicit ID list and gated behind organizer. RANGE CAME FROM http.ServeContent RATHER THAN AN IMPLEMENTATION - it already handles Range, If-Range, multi-range refusal, Content-Range and 416 correctly. The handler was doing io.Copy; it now type-asserts the store io.ReadCloser to an io.ReadSeeker (an *os.File in practice) and delegates, so OpenResourceContent interface is unchanged and a non-seekable source falls back to a full copy without ranges, the honest outcome rather than a wrong one. validation: go test ./... (incl. template and task tests)
npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build
notes: A template is an ordinary note carrying a fenced note-template block declaring prompt: lines; a task is a checkbox list item extracted on read. No schema change and no migration - templates are notes and tasks are computed. THE CLOSED VOCABULARY IS THE WHOLE SAFETY ARGUMENT: a placeholder name is either a declared prompt or one of date, time, datetime, title, notebook, and anything else is an error naming the alternatives; an open vocabulary would be an expression language, which is exactly what E7 spent a slice refusing, and the placeholder pattern allows only letters, digits and underscore so it cannot look like a call or a path even by accident. SUBSTITUTION IS ONE PASS AND THAT IS A SECURITY PROPERTY RATHER THAN AN OPTIMISATION: a supplied value containing {{date}} is inserted literally and never re-scanned, so a value cannot introduce a placeholder, cannot reach an automatic name it was not given, and cannot recurse - everything a caller supplies is data, asserted directly. An unknown placeholder is an error ON THE TEMPLATE reported at listing time rather than at creation, because a typo like {{onwer}} discovered when someone tries to use the template is discovered too late; malformed templates are listed with their error rather than hidden since the author is who needs to find them. A missing value is refused rather than left blank and an undeclared value is refused rather than ignored; an automatic name cannot be prompted for, since two sources for one name would make which wins a coin toss. TASKS ARE COMPUTED ON READ FOR A CONCRETE REASON: document_blocks stores a content hash and byte offsets but NOT block text, so there is nothing to query for is-this-checked and the body has to be read either way - which makes extraction a whole-library scan of the same shape and cost as lint, exactly what the decision anticipated (no table until a query needs one a scan cannot serve). A LIKE prefilter skips notes that cannot contain a checkbox before any body is parsed, and document_id/notebook_id turn the scan into a small one for the common case. Counts stay complete when rows are capped, the same contract lint examples have. THE IDENTITY PROPERTY HAS AN HONEST LIMIT, ASSERTED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: a task keeps its block ID through edits AROUND it - the test inserts a paragraph above and below and also asserts the ordinal moved, so it cannot pass by the task having stayed put - but the checkbox is part of the block text, since - [ ] x reaches the parser as [ ] x, so TICKING A TASK CHANGES ITS DERIVED ID. That is the block model working as documented rather than a defect, and the answer is the one the block model already has: an author-written ^marker outranks the derived ID and survives the rewrite. The assertion is deliberately worded to fail loudly if the block model contract ever changes, because a silent change there would quietly alter what every task link means. MCP: list_templates and list_tasks under read-only, create_from_template under editor - and F2 whole-set scope test caught all three the moment they were registered.

task: Graph views that stay readable at scale

notes: Three deliverables replaced the global canvas: a LOCAL GRAPH in the GUI (depth 1-2, ceiling stated, no graph library because a neighbourhood at that depth is tens of nodes and the traversal is already bounded SQL), the HUBS REPORT WRITTEN AS A READ-ONLY NOTE in a new builtin Reports notebook, and CSV NODE/EDGE EXPORT (CLI-only). No schema change and no migration - bootstrap INSERT OR IGNORE reaches an existing database on the next open. THE PREDICATE IS NAMED IsReadOnlyNotebook AND NOT IsBuiltinNotebook, AND THAT NAMING IS LOAD-BEARING: one predicate replaced thirteen hard-coded NotebookID == HelpNotebookID comparisons, so Reports was protected the day it was added, but two different sets exist - undeletable is Help, Reports AND Notes (nb.Builtin OR the default ID), while read-only is Help and Reports alone. Notes is builtin = 0 in the database precisely because its content is the user's, and a test pins that DefaultNotebookID is NOT read-only, because widening the set by reaching for the more familiar word would have silently excluded most of a library from the graph report, from publications and from lint. THE GRAPH REPORT WAS MEASURING SOMETHING OTHER THAN THE LIVE LIBRARY AND ONE OF THE TWO MISSING FILTERS WAS A PRE-EXISTING DEFECT: the row set excluded trashed notes so one was never ranked, but the in-degree subquery placed no condition on the link's SOURCE, and soft delete deliberately leaves document_links intact so a restore can use them - so a note in the Trash kept propping up the in-degree of everything it had linked to, and a note linked only from the Trash was never reported as an orphan. The second filter is what lets the report live in the library it measures: it links to every hub it ranks, so without it writing the report would change the ranking the next generation sees, and excluding the report from its own RANKING would not have fixed that because the links would still count. Both ends of every counted edge are filtered rather than just the source, so link_count finally means what its documentation always claimed. Rows in read-only notebooks are not measured either, or every Help note would have arrived as a fresh orphan the moment the link filter started working. MUTATION-VERIFIED: restoring the original in-degree subquery makes both new tests fail with the exact numbers the defect produced. TRAVERSAL FOLLOWS THE SAME PREDICATE WITH ONE EXEMPTION THAT EARNS ITS KEEP: a read-only note's links are ignored unless that note is one of the ROOTS asked about - otherwise every hub's local graph would show the report one hop away (noise in exactly the view this slice argues stays useful at scale), but without the exemption opening the report or any Help page would render an empty graph, a regression dressed up as consistency. Verified in the browser against real data: Kitchen Plan's local graph omits the report while the database confirms the report DOES carry a resolved link to it, so the absence is the filter working rather than a missing link. PUBLICATION EXCLUDES READ-ONLY NOTEBOOKS BY DEFAULT, reported in the dry run as read_only_notebook:<id> so it is visible rather than silent, as a rule inside the target's default policy rather than a user-facing field (not something a user should configure, and a field invites getting it wrong), not overridable in v0.6 because adding an opt-in later is easy and removing a leak is not. Full archive and subset transfer keep both notebooks for real reasons: the first is a backup and must restore faithfully, the second moves notes between the user's own databases. LINT SKIPS CONTENT CHECKS IN READ-ONLY NOTEBOOKS BUT NOT projection_backlog - that one says the search index is behind rather than that a note needs editing, and hiding it would hide a real operational problem for nothing; the distinction is pinned by a test so it reads as deliberate rather than as a place the filter was forgotten. VISIBLE CHANGE: on this repository's own seeded Help notebook it removes 71 unresolved-link findings that notriosctl fix structurally could not repair and the user could not edit, and report_sha256 changes with them. MARKDOWN ESCAPING COULD NOT SAVE A HOSTILE TITLE: the first implementation escaped [ and ] in the link text, and Notrios' own link parser forbids ] inside link text EVEN BACKSLASH-ESCAPED (the pattern is \[([^\]\n]*)\]\(), so the escaped form produced a link the store could not resolve - a broken link in a generated note, in the user's lint report, blamed on a note they cannot edit. A title carrying ] is now written verbatim beside a short ([open](...)) link rather than altered to fit; both branches are asserted, because a fallback that never fires and one that always fires are both wrong. NOTHING NEW ON THE MCP PATH: regenerating the report scans the whole collection and overwrites a note, and export writes files at a path the caller names, so both join the withheld list with the reason recorded and TestNoScopeReachesWholeLibraryOperations now names them so a future tool cannot arrive quietly. BROWSER VERIFICATION FOUND A DEFECT THE TESTS DID NOT: the editor's read-only badge was hard-coded to 'Read-only Help note' and rendered that on a note in Reports - wrong in the one place a reader looks to find out why they cannot type. It now names the note's actual notebook, with a test for each.

task: Job control plane for bulk work
validation: go test ./... (incl. store, runner, REST, MCP and CLI job tests)
openapi parse (63 paths; a duplicate JobStatus schema was found and removed)
npx tsc --noEmit && npx vitest run (155 tests) && npm run build
end-to-end: 4,000-note vault import watched from a second process, cancelled, resumed, hard-killed and shown interrupted, read over REST and MCP
notes: Schema v18 jobs table; the two batching importers and archive export record into it; notriosctl jobs list/status/show/cancel, three REST routes and two read-only MCP tools read and stop it. GET /api/v1/jobs/{job_id} stopped being a stub that answered 'unknown' for every ID. NARROWER THAN THE PLAN BULLET IN ONE PLACE AND THE USER WAS TOLD: the bullet said 'MCP may start and watch a job', but NOTHING STARTS A JOB OVER REST OR MCP. Every kind this build runs names a filesystem path, and the standing v0.4 decision restated in SECURITY_REVIEW.md and hardened in F3 and F5 is that no REST or MCP surface accepts an archive path or streams archive bytes. PUTTING A JOB RECORD AROUND AN OPERATION DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT THE OPERATION DOES, so a start route would have reopened exactly the boundary F3 recorded a reason for closing; the same bullet's second half ('bulk bytes never travel this way') is why that is the right reading. Cancel is offered over REST and CLI but withheld from MCP separately: safe for the data, but stopping a person's four-hour import is their decision. INTERRUPTED IS DERIVED, NEVER STORED. A process that dies cannot write its own epitaph, so a job left running with a heartbeat older than two minutes is reported interrupted at read time. A sweeper that WROTE it would have to decide another process is dead, and two Notrios processes against one database - notriosd serving the GUI while notriosctl imports - would take turns declaring each other's work over. Deriving it also means a merely-slow job can come back and finish normally, which is asserted. FinishJob refuses 'interrupted' as an argument: a process able to write it is a process that was not interrupted. RECORDS PERSIST ACROSS A RESTART, THE WORK DOES NOT, AND THIS WAS VERIFIED ON REAL DATA: a 4,000-note Obsidian import cancelled from a second process stopped at 1,225 notes (a clean 49x25 batch multiple), recorded cancelled, exited 4 - and rerunning the same command STARTED AT 1,250 and finished all 4,000. The importer's own import_checkpoints row is the resume mechanism; a second one layered on top would give two answers to one question, which is why there is no resume column. THE EXISTING AfterBatch SEAM WAS ALREADY THE RIGHT PLACE TO CANCEL: it runs AFTER the batch is committed and the checkpoint saved, and returning an error aborts the import, so progress reporting and the stop signal share one hook and stopping leaves a state the next run resumes from. Archive export has no such boundary, so it uses the other mechanism - the runner owns a context, cancelling it aborts at the next store read, and because the manifest is written last and IS the completion marker a stopped export leaves nothing that could pass as complete. BOTH ROUTES CLASSIFY IDENTICALLY as cancelled rather than failed, because they are the same event arriving two ways and an operator should not be sent hunting for a fault that does not exist. MUTATION-VERIFIED: removing the cancelled case makes both halves fail with state = failed. PARAMETERS ARE STORED, THE COMMAND IS RENDERED. Raw argv would have captured local paths and any secret that happened to be on the command line into the database, and a stored string cannot improve when a flag is renamed. Each parameter carries a path flag, which is what lets notriosctl jobs show --command print a runnable command locally while REST and MCP return NO parameters at all; the disclosure test asserts against the real value (/home/someone/Private Vault) so re-adding the field under another name fails too. Rendering is tested against a hostile path (/tmp/it's here; rm -rf /) because a rendered command exists to be pasted into a shell, and a separate test walks every kind store.JobKinds() knows and fails if the CLI has no command for it. THE MCP VIEW DROPS TWO FIELDS REST KEEPS, both because their values routinely contain a local path: the parameters and the free-text error, since a filesystem failure reads like 'open /home/someone/private/x: permission denied'. The state is still reported with a pointer to notriosctl jobs show. A summary crosses because it is counts by construction. NO SCHEDULER; THE EXIT CODES ARE WHY: 0 succeeded, 1 failed, 2 usage, 3 running, 4 cancelled, 5 no such job, 6 interrupted, with --wait blocking until settled - enough for job-a && job-b. 6 IS DELIBERATELY NOT 1 because an interruption usually just needs the command run again, which is not the response to a failure, and a test asserts no state collides with 2 (usage everywhere else in this CLI). Ctrl-C requests cancellation on the first signal so the record settles as cancelled rather than lying 'running' for two minutes; a second signal still kills the process. THREE DEFECTS FOUND WHILE BUILDING: listing was not actually newest-first, because CURRENT_TIMESTAMP has one-second resolution and the tiebreak fell to the random job ID - it now orders by rowid, which IS insertion order; jobs status <id> --wait exited 2 with a bare usage dump, since Go's flag package stops at the first positional, so the refusal now names the flag and says it must come first; and openapi.yaml carried a DUPLICATE JobStatus schema where the stale placeholder definition was silently overriding the new one.
